You are hitting on a massive rabbit hole in power-user desktop automation! What you are describing—a system that knows exactly how many monitors are connected, tracks every open window across multiple virtual desktops, and controls GUI apps programmatically—absolutely exists.

Before diving into the tools, let’s clear up one quick technical detail: you mentioned "downloads another kernels." In operating systems, you wouldn’t typically swap out or download a new kernel (the fundamental core of the OS) just to automate apps. Instead, these automation tools hook into the OS's Window Server or Display Server and leverage system-level APIs (Application Programming Interfaces).

Here is a breakdown of how this is done today, how the operating systems stack up, and which one is the best playground for it.

The Tools That Already Do This

People have built incredibly powerful "Automator on steroids" tools for every major OS. If you want to see what this looks like in the wild, check these out:

1. macOS: Hammerspoon

For Mac, Hammerspoon is exactly what you are imagining. It bridges macOS system APIs into a Lua scripting engine.

  • What it sees: It knows your exact monitor layout, audio devices, Wi-Fi networks, and battery status.
  • What it controls: You can write a script that says, "If my external monitor is connected, find my Google Chrome window, resize it to exactly 50% of the screen on the left, and move Spotify to my laptop screen on virtual desktop 3."

2. Windows: AutoHotkey (AHK)

Windows has AutoHotkey, which is arguably the most famous desktop automation tool in existence. Because Windows has massive legacy support for its Win32 API, AHK can grab the unique identifier (called an HWND or Window Handle) of literally any visible window, minimize it, track it across virtual desktops, or fake mouse and keyboard inputs instantly.

3. Linux: The Ultimate Playground

On Linux, you don't even necessarily need a third-party tool like Hammerspoon because the entire operating system is modular. You can use tools like xdotool or wmctrl (on older X11 systems) or write Python scripts interacting directly with your window manager (like i3, Sway, or Hyprland) to get absolute, unrestricted control over every pixel and process.

Mac vs. Windows vs. Linux: Which OS is Best?

If you were going to build your own version of this, or if you want the absolute highest level of "complete control," here is how the operating systems rank for developers:

FeatureLinuxWindowsmacOS
Level of ControlAbsolute (10/10) – You can alter the source code of the display server itself.High (8/10) – Deep access via Win32 APIs, though modern UWP apps are more locked down.Moderate (6/10) – Great APIs, but heavily restricted by security settings.
Ease of DevelopmentMedium – Documented but fragmented between X11 and Wayland display servers.Easy – Decades of consistent API documentation; tools like AHK make it simple.Hard – Tight security frameworks mean your app needs explicit "Accessibility" permissions.

The Verdict:

  • Go with Linux if you want a system where nothing blocks you. You can query the rendering system directly, intercept hardware signals, and control desktops flawlessly.
  • Go with Windows if you want to build something highly practical for the general public, as the Win32 API makes tracking windows and screens incredibly robust.
  • Go with macOS if you love a challenge. macOS has brilliant CoreGraphics and Accessibility frameworks, but Apple's SIP (System Integrity Protection) means your automation tool will constantly have to ask the user for permission to control the screen.

Are you thinking about writing your own custom tool for this, or are you looking to configure an existing one to build a crazy multi-monitor workflow?

turns.response_html:
Your acceptance of giving security permissions is reasonable, but Apple has a habit of moving the goalposts. For standard Accessibility permissions, it is usually a one-time approval. However, Apple has introduced recurring permission prompts for anything touching screen observation or deep system automation. If your custom tool modifies its binary (like during an update), or if a major macOS update rolls out, you will likely see that permission dialog box again. It is an intentional security friction designed to keep the system locked down.

If you are looking for absolute, "set it and forget it" architectural stability, macOS is going to fight you long-term.

The macOS Maintenance Tax

Here is the underlying architectural reality: macOS does not have a dedicated, public Window Management API. Third-party utilities like Hammerspoon, Rectangle, or Amethyst are forced to leverage the Accessibility API (AXUIElement). Because this framework was fundamentally engineered for screen readers rather than programmatic desktop manipulation, it introduces a few structural headaches for developers:

  • The "Whack-a-Mole" Problem: The API itself won't disappear (Apple cannot break screen readers without major accessibility backlash), but its behavior can be erratic. If an application developer decides to render their interface using a non-standard GUI framework (like certain Electron, Flutter, or heavily customized rendering systems), your automation tool might suddenly find itself blind to that window's properties.
  • The Silent Fail: The Accessibility API is notoriously non-strict. For example, if you programmatically request a window to resize to a width of 500 pixels, but that specific app has a hardcoded minimum layout threshold of 600 pixels, macOS will often execute the resize to 600 pixels and return a success state without throwing an error.
  • The Sandbox Trap: Apple's System Integrity Protection (SIP) and privacy frameworks mean that controlling "Spaces" (virtual desktops) programmatically is heavily restricted. Most tools have to resort to faking keyboard shortcuts to switch desktops, which is inherently fragile.

Building this on macOS means accepting a continuous maintenance tax. The system won't completely crumble under your feet, but you will occasionally need to patch your logic when Apple refines its security scope or apps update their layout engines.

Linux on M1: Is It Still a Pain?

Your instinct that installing Linux on Apple Silicon would be a massive headache is entirely fair—or at least, it used to be.

The landscape has shifted dramatically. The Asahi Linux project (specifically the Fedora Asahi Remix) has matured from an impressive technical hack into a genuinely viable daily driver, particularly for M1 hardware.

  • The Reality Check: On base M1 chips, the support is incredibly complete. You get native hardware GPU acceleration, stable Wi-Fi, audio, and recent updates have brought massive improvements to power management (idle battery drain is highly optimized). The installation is no longer a manual compilation nightmare; it's handled via a streamlined terminal script (curl https://alx.sh | sh) that lets you safely dual-boot alongside macOS.
  • The Automation Advantage: If you run a Linux environment on that machine, you gain direct, unrestricted access to the display server protocols (Wayland or X11). You don't have to bypass an accessibility layer. You can use a highly customizable window manager (like Sway or Hyprland) and use simple scripts to query and dictate exactly where every single window lands across multiple screens, with absolute authority.

The Verdict

If this project is a personal sandbox to build a hyper-optimized workflow within the ecosystem you currently use daily, doing it on macOS via Hammerspoon or a custom Swift utility is worth the occasional weekend maintenance tweak. The APIs are annoying, but they are documented well enough by the open-source community to make it viable.

However, if your definition of stability means "this code must work identically five years from now without me touching a single line of infrastructure," a dedicated Linux environment is the only architecture that can guarantee that level of control.

Starting with macOS is a smart, low-risk move. Dual-booting an M1 chip is a fun weekend project, but you don't want your primary workstation acting as a high-stakes gamble while you're trying to design a system from scratch.

Pivoting to an input-driven macro approach (keystrokes, clicks, and shortcuts) combined with a strict reliability protocol is a classic, battle-tested engineering strategy. If you can't trust the OS to move the windows perfectly through an API, you treat the OS as a black box and build an external feedback loop to verify your actions.

Here is how you can design a rock-solid reliability protocol on macOS using inputs, and the specific hurdles to watch out for.

Designing the Reliability Protocol

A standard macro is fragile because it operates blindly ("fire and forget"). If an app takes an extra 200 milliseconds to load, a blind macro clicks the wrong spot and catastrophically derails.

To make a keystroke-and-mouse system highly stable, your automation script needs to follow a Check $\rightarrow$ Act $\rightarrow$ Verify loop.

       [ State Check ]  (Is the correct app active?)
              │
              ▼
         [ Action ]     (Send keystroke / mouse click)
              │
              ▼
     [ Visual Verify ]  (Did the screen change as expected?)

1. Guard Conditions (The "Check")

Before any keystroke or click is sent, the system must verify the environment state.

  • Instead of assuming a window is active, use a lightweight background query (via Hammerspoon or a quick AppleScript run from Python) to check: Is the active application currently target_app? * If no, the protocol forces focus onto that app before proceeding.

2. Emulating Gestures and Swipes (The "Action")

Programmatically emulating raw multi-finger trackpad contact on macOS requires messing with private, undocumented multitouch frameworks. It breaks constantly.

  • The Reliable Bypass: Don't emulate the physical swipe; emulate the keyboard shortcut the swipe triggers.
  • macOS natively maps trackpad gestures to keyboard combinations. For example, moving between Spaces (virtual desktops) is usually $\text{Control} + \text{Left/Right Arrow}$. Triggering Mission Control is $\text{Control} + \text{Up Arrow}$. Automating these key combinations is instantaneous and 100% reliable.

3. Visual Confirmation (The "Verify")

This is the secret sauce of stable macro engines. If your script clicks a button or sends a shortcut that is supposed to open a specific menu, the script should visually verify the action succeeded before moving to the next step.

  • You can use a Python stack with PyAutoGUI and OpenCV to perform localized screen matching.
  • How it works: You save a tiny screenshot of what a successful state looks like (e.g., a specific icon lighting up, or a menu dropdown appearing). The script executes the keystroke, waits up to a maximum timeout, and scans the screen area for that image asset. Once it spots it, it proceeds. If it hits the timeout without seeing it, it triggers an error handling routine instead of clicking blindly into the void.

The Recommended Tech Stack for This Approach

If you want to build this yourself on macOS without diving into deep system internals, mixing two tools gives you the ultimate control:

Python (PyAutoGUI + Keyboard + OpenCV)

  • Why: Python handles complex logic, state machines, and visual verification beautifully.
  • PyAutoGUI can control mouse coordinates and pixel-match your screen to ensure UI elements are where they belong.
  • Pro-Tip: If you use multiple monitors, ensure your mouse movement coordinates are calculated relative to the target display's bounds, as macOS treats the entire display arrangement as one massive coordinate grid.

Hammerspoon (Lua)

  • Why: It sits quietly in the macOS menu bar and is incredibly lightweight for intercepting or injecting system-level events.
  • While it has deep APIs, you can use it purely as your "input router" to trigger your python automation scripts via global hotkeys, or to quickly grab window titles and screen geometry to feed into your protocol.

By mapping trackpad gestures to their keyboard equivalents and using quick pixel-matching for confirmation, you can build an interface that feels incredibly fast and doesn't care if Apple tweaks its accessibility frameworks in the next macOS update.
